title: When Is "Good Enough" Actually Good Enough?
author: Nir Eyal and Jasmine Eyal
summary: Nir Eyal and his daughter Jasmine Eyal co-write about the paralysis they experienced perfecting a live program presentation, and the checklist, called END, they built afterward to know when to stop revising. The framework asks three yes/no questions, whether continued effort is the best use of time (Effort cost), whether the next improvement can be named specifically rather than felt vaguely (Name improvement), and whether more work is likely to yield materially better results (Decreasing returns), with three "no" answers signaling the task is genuinely finished. They ground each letter in research: a 2025 meta-analysis of over 9,000 people found that perfectionism driven by high standards improved performance while perfectionism driven by fear of judgment did not, despite equal hours worked, and a 2023 study found that time pressure pushes people toward small incremental tweaks rather than original thinking. The piece frames the pursuit of perfection not as a virtue but as a way to avoid the discomfort of hard choices, and argues that naming the specific reason to keep working (or stop) replaces exhaustion as the true measure of good work.
points: Introduces the END framework (Effort cost, Name improvement, Decreasing returns), a three-question checklist for deciding when a task is genuinely finished rather than merely abandoned from exhaustion.

Cites a 2025 meta-analysis of 9,000+ people distinguishing two types of perfectionism: pursuing high standards improved performance, while working from doubt and fear of judgment did not, despite equal hours invested.
Cites a 2023 study of 203 employees showing moderate time pressure shifts people toward incremental tweaks and away from original thinking, and heavy time pressure suppresses both kinds of thinking.

Reframes perfectionism as an avoidance strategy: 'The allure of achieving perfection is enticing. It is also an illusion we use to rationalize avoiding difficult choices, hard questions, and uncomfortable feelings.'
quotes: We needed a better way to know when good enough was actually good and enough. So we created a checklist we now use whenever we're not sure whether to persist or move on.

A 2025 meta-analysis involving over 9,000 people found two types of perfectionism associated with working longer hours, but only one associated with better performance. Those chasing high standards saw improved outcomes. Those driven by doubts, mistakes, and others' judgments did not, despite working just as long.
If you can't name the specific change and the associated improvement, add an N.

A 2023 study of 203 employees and their supervisors found that moderate time pressure pushes people toward incremental improvements and away from more original thinking. Under heavy time pressure, both kinds of thinking decline.
The allure of achieving perfection is enticing. It is also an illusion we use to rationalize avoiding difficult choices, hard questions, and uncomfortable feelings.
